Title: proposal: decouple export data formats used by compiler and x/tools

Body: This is @cherrymui's idea.

**Background:** Export data is the compact binary notation for serialized type information: conceptually it is a serialized types.Package. There are two different formats today: the unified (u) format written and read by the compiler, and the indexed (i) format written and read by x/tools (incl. gopls). However, the x/tools reader must also be capable of reading u format because `go list -export` runs the compiler to generate export data files. This creates a complex and inconvenient coupling between the compiler and x/tools.

**Proposal:** Let's split the two formats apart. The compiler would read and write only `u` format written by the exact same version of the toolchain. This would allow it to evolve independently: any commit on any given day would be free to change the reader and writer. We would provide no supported way to read the compiler's format; even its existence would be an internal implementation detail.

The x/tools format would read and write only `i` format; however, it would still need to retain the ability to read files produced by `go list -export`. So, we could change `go list -export` to run not cmd/compile but a new frontend tool, cmd/export, based on go/ast + go/types + vendor/x/tools, that simply reads, parses, and type-checks Go source files, reading export data for dependencies and writing it out for the current package. (The cmd/export tool should be straightforward to write: it's basically unitchecker with the analysis parts ripped out, accepting its command-line arguments in cmd/compile not cmd/vet form).

The only unknown quantity is the go/importer package. Today it may be used to read files named by `go list -export`; since these would in future be produced by cmd/export, go/importer would use the vendored x/tools reader. But it's possible that some users are also using it to parse .a files produced by the compiler that they found some other way. (I vaguely recall seeing such file names in the output of `go list -json` but I cannot now find them. `go help install` talks about package files being installed, but I don't know exactly what that implies.) We need to investigate who would be broken if we stopped making go/importer support compiler export data files.

When a language change affects exported types, the process would be:
1. add support to go/types{,2}. Now you can use the feature in single-package tests of go/types and/or the compiler.
2. add support to the compiler and its export data reader/writer. Now you can use the feature in multi-package tests of the compiler.
3. add support to x/tools reader and writer.
4. vendor x/tools into GOROOT. Now Go developers' `go list -export` would be emitting the new format (whether or not the package actually uses new language features). Any x/tools-based commands installed on their $PATH would need to be re-built with a version of x/tools later than step 3.
5. Go release. At this point all users of the new toolchain would be using the new format. Tools binaries on their PATH would need updating.

Several people have asked why not guarantee backward compatibility of the x/tools file format so that installed x/tools-based tools are not broken by each toolchain update. This is appealing, but in general it is impossible: if a package makes use of a new language feature that cannot yet be written, there is really nothing sound that the reader can do other than report a version skew error. It might seem gentler to the user not to report an error until we actually encounter a usage of the new language feature (not just the newer file version number), but typically the new feature will be quickly adopted in low-level packages, so there is little practical benefit to reporting the error lazily.

Title: [Inductor][CPU] Full-buffer clone for generalized_scatter followed by index_put and input copy-back

Body: ## Human commentary

After reviewing the prior GMES analysis and benchmark results, I asked Codex to file this issue. The latest PyTorch nightly still reproduces the full-buffer clone, and the isolated result is large enough that I believe a narrowly scoped Inductor fix is worth discussing upstream. I would especially appreciate guidance on whether this should be a focused follow-up or coordinated with #190548.

 
 AI-assisted technical report 

> **AI assistance disclosure:** Codex ran the reproducer, inspected the relevant Inductor source and existing issues/PRs, and drafted the technical report below. The submitting human reviewed the summarized diagnosis and measurements before authorizing this issue.

## 🐛 Describe the bug

When a compiled function composes a normal slice mutation with an indexed mutation of the same graph input, functionalization produces a graph shaped like:

 [CODE_BLOCK] generalized_scatter(input, ...)
 -> index_put/index_copy
 -> copy_(input, ...)
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

Inductor leaves the `generalized_scatter` functional, cloning the entire input buffer on every invocation. The two mutations are allocation-free or nearly allocation-free when compiled separately; the full-buffer clone appears only when they are composed.

The latest nightly's `should_reinplace_scatter()` recognizes a direct `generalized_scatter -> copy_(input)` relationship, but not the case where an inplaceable indexed mutation is between the scatter and the final copy-back:

[URL]

### Minimal operation pattern

 [CODE_BLOCK] import torch

FIELD_ELEMENTS = 51_520
INDEXED_ELEMENTS = 99

def composed(field, delta, indices, gain):
 field[1:-1].add_(delta)
 values = torch.index_select(field, 0, indices) * gain
 field.index_copy_(0, indices, values)

torch.set_num_threads(1)
torch.set_num_interop_threads(1)

base = torch.linspace(0.25, 1.25, FIELD_ELEMENTS, dtype=torch.float64)
delta = torch.linspace(-0.01, 0.01, FIELD_ELEMENTS - 2, dtype=torch.float64)
indices = torch.arange(0, 2 * INDEXED_ELEMENTS, 2, dtype=torch.int64)
gain = torch.linspace(0.99, 1.01, INDEXED_ELEMENTS, dtype=torch.float64)

compiled = torch.compile(composed, fullgraph=True)

expected = base.clone()
actual = base.clone()
for _ in range(5):
 composed(expected, delta, indices, gain)
 compiled(actual, delta, indices, gain)

torch.testing.assert_close(actual, expected, rtol=0, atol=0)
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

A standalone reproducer with allocation tracing, timing, exact-equivalence checks, isolated ablations, and a public `as_strided` comparison is available here:

[URL]

Example commands:

 [CODE_BLOCK] OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 \
python torch_inductor_composed_mutation.py \
 --assert-affected \
 --profile-calls 5 \
 --timing-repeats 5 \
 --timing-calls 100 \
 --equivalence-calls 5
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

The script also has a private diagnostic `--force-reinplace` switch. It replaces the scatter profitability predicate with `True` only to isolate the missed reinplace decision; it is **not** a proposed or safe general-purpose fix.

## Results

Measured on an M1 Pro with one CPU thread using `torch==2.15.0.dev20260829` (`5b77b6ed10d79b06e978168940350a2a998eb9ce`):

| Variant | Median time | Positive allocation per call | Full-field allocation |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Current composed graph | 61.33 us | 412,160 bytes | 1 x 412,160 bytes |
| Diagnostic forced reinplace | 24.70 us | 792 bytes | 0 |
| Public `as_strided` formulation | 23.93 us | 792 bytes | 0 |

The diagnostic removes the full-field clone and reduces the isolated kernel time by about 59.7% (2.48x). Eager and compiled results remained bitwise equal after five repeated mutations.

Useful ablations from the same run:

- Slice/stencil mutation alone: no positive allocation.
- Indexed material mutation alone: 792 bytes per call, no full-field allocation.
- Composed ordinary-slice mutation: 412,160-byte full-field allocation per call.
- Equivalent public `as_strided` composition: no full-field allocation.

This is an isolated-kernel result, not a claim of a 59.7% end-to-end GMES speedup.

## Expected behavior

When alias/liveness analysis establishes that reinplacing is safe, Inductor should avoid the full-buffer clone for a `generalized_scatter` whose result flows through a known inplaceable indexed mutation and is finally copied back to the same graph input.

A deliberately narrow first implementation could:

1. Follow a single-user chain from `_generalized_scatter`.
2. Initially allow only already-known inplaceable `aten.index_put.default` / corresponding indexed-update forms.
3. Require the final result to be copied back to the original placeholder or `get_attr`.
4. Preserve the existing alias and liveness checks as the safety gate.
5. Include negative tests for an additional consumer, copy-back to a different input, and metadata/alias mismatch.

## Related work / possible overlap

- #184542 / #184263 handle a layout-preserving `graph input -> view -> index_put -> inverse view -> copy_` pattern. The pattern here has a `_generalized_scatter` feeding the indexed mutation instead.
- #190548 handles `copy_(base, _generalized_scatter(base, getitem(triton_kernel_wrapper_functional(...)), views))` for read-write Triton view arguments. It touches the same reinplace machinery, but does not cover `_generalized_scatter -> index_put -> copy_(original input)`.
- Search terms including `generalized_scatter index_put copy_`, `reinplace scatter index_put`, and `full-buffer clone reinplace` did not find an exact existing issue.

Would maintainers prefer this as a focused follow-up to #190548, or should the recognition be generalized in that PR's infrastructure?

* Ensure excluded files do not appear in Call Hierarchy results.
* Reuse existing VS Code file-exclusion configuration where appropriate.
* Add tests covering file and pattern-based exclusions.
* Document the new configuration option.

* A user can configure a file/pattern to be excluded.
* The excluded file is not shown in Call Hierarchy results.
* Existing Call Hierarchy behavior remains unchanged when no exclusions are configured.

where we say: "unsafe by design, has numerous known security issues, is not maintained, and should not be used".

We should just follow through with our deprecation, and remove the code in the standard fashion of carving out a module, tagging it, and deleting the code.

Title: XLA rewrites exp(a) * exp(b) to exp(a + b), changing NaN to 1.0

Body: ### Issue type

Bug

### Have you reproduced the bug with TensorFlow Nightly?

Yes

### Source

binary

### TensorFlow version

`tf-nightly 2.22.0-dev20260713` (`v1.12.1-142315-gfb9cdf75cf2`)

### Custom code

Yes

### OS platform and distribution

Ubuntu 20.04.4 LTS (x86_64)

### Mobile device

No response

### Python version

3.11.15

### Bazel version

No response

### GCC/compiler version

No response

### CUDA/cuDNN version

CPU-only reproducer

### GPU model and memory

CPU-only reproducer

### Current behavior?

With `jit_compile=True`, XLA returns `1.0` for `exp(100.0) * exp(-100.0)`, while eager execution and a non-XLA `tf.function` both return `NaN`.

The optimized HLO rewrites the expression from two exponentials followed by a multiply:

 [CODE_BLOCK] %exponential.3 = f32[1]{0} exponential(%arg0.1)
%exponential.4 = f32[1]{0} exponential(%arg1.1)
ROOT %multiply.5 = f32[1]{0} multiply(%exponential.3, %exponential.4)
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

to one addition followed by one exponential:

 [CODE_BLOCK] %add.1 = f32[1]{0} add(%param_0.1, %param_1)
ROOT %exponential.1 = f32[1]{0} exponential(%add.1)
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

This corresponds to the AlgebraicSimplifier rule `exp(LHS) * exp(RHS) => exp(LHS + RHS)`. The transformation is not equivalent at floating-point overflow/underflow boundaries: the original expression evaluates as an overflowing exponential multiplied by an underflowed exponential, whereas the rewritten expression evaluates as `exp(0)`.

As a control, setting `XLA_FLAGS=--xla_disable_hlo_passes=algsimp` makes the XLA result `NaN` and preserves the two exponentials and multiply in optimized HLO.

I expected the XLA-compiled function to preserve the observable eager/graph result for this expression, or for this rewrite to be guarded when it changes non-finite behavior.

### Standalone code to reproduce the issue

 [CODE_BLOCK] import os

os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = ""
os.environ["TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL"] = "2"

import tensorflow as tf

def expression(left, right):
 return tf.exp(left) * tf.exp(right)

left = tf.constant([100.0], dtype=tf.float32)
right = tf.constant([-100.0], dtype=tf.float32)

graph_expression = tf.function(expression)
xla_expression = tf.function(expression, jit_compile=True)

print("TensorFlow:", tf.__version__)
print("eager:", expression(left, right).numpy())
print("graph:", graph_expression(left, right).numpy())
print("xla: ", xla_expression(left, right).numpy())
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### Relevant log output

 [CODE_BLOCK] TensorFlow: 2.22.0-dev20260713
eager: [nan]
graph: [nan]
xla: [1.]
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

The rewrite is implemented in `AlgebraicSimplifierVisitor::HandleMultiply`:

`Could not download the nemotron-3.5-asr-streaming-0.6b speech-to-text model, which can happen on networks that block the model registry. You can install it from a downloaded package instead.`

The VS Code website mentions the following:
`If network restrictions prevent VS Code from downloading the on-device model, download the official CPU model package separately. Then run Chat: Install Dictation Model from Local Package... and select the ZIP file or prepared model folder.`

It is, however, not that trivial as to how to get this up and running manually. Maybe the documentation could be improved a bit in this regard. In any case, I'll describe how I got it to work eventually in case it is useful to others. I am not sure whether I have missed something completely that would simplify manual installation, but that would in any case then be useful to add to the documentation.

# Manual installation & issues
The first minor issue is that when browsing for the model, VS Code does not allow to select ".zip" files.

When searching for this model online, you'll only find the Hugging Face repository of this model and the NVIDIA webpage, which refers to the same Hugging Face page. The problem is that the Hugging Face version of the model is not accepted by VS Code as it must be a specific ONNX version of the model. It was a bit difficult to find out how to obtain a suitable model. I now found a Microsoft blogpost on live transcriptions that provided some guidance. The code I now use to download the model:
 [CODE_BLOCK] """
This script downloads a streaming speech model using Foundry Local.

Requirements:
 pip install foundry-local-sdk
"""

from pathlib import Path

from foundry_local_sdk import Configuration, FoundryLocalManager

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Initialize Foundry Local
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

cache_dir = Path(".") / "nemotron"
config = Configuration(
 app_name="fetch-vscode-dictation-model",
 model_cache_dir=str(cache_dir),
)
FoundryLocalManager.initialize(config)
manager = FoundryLocalManager.instance

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Download and load the streaming speech model
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

model = manager.catalog.get_model("nemotron-3.5-asr-streaming-0.6b")

if not model.is_cached:
 print("Downloading model...")
 model.download(lambda progress: print(f"\r Progress: {progress:.1f}%", end="", flush=True))
 print("\n Download complete.")

print(f"Model: {model.id}")
print(f"Prepared model folder: {model.get_path()}")
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

Selecting the cache directory of this model is accepted by VS Code and its files are saved to `%APPDATA%\Code\chatDictationModels\`. However, dictation still would not work as the same error message kept popping up. I found out that VS Code also needs a Foundry Local runtime that might be downloaded together with the model normally, which I cannot check myself. VS Code will, misleadingly, keep showing the error that the model must first be downloaded manually instead.

I now circumvented this by also downloading the runtime files manually here:
[URL]
And extracting the files, such that:
 [CODE_BLOCK] %APPDATA%\Code\chatDictationRuntime\1.2.3\
├── .complete-win32-x64
├── prebuilds\win32-x64\foundry_local_napi.node
└── foundry-local-core\win32-x64\ (Foundry Local + onnxruntime DLLs)
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 
Finally, the `.complete-win32-x64` file must be added manually to the directory above. It's contents must be set to `1.2.3`. After that, the dictation function started working for me.

### Current behavior?

## Current behavior

I verified this issue locally on 2026-03-24 by running the original reproducer in the `tf_test` conda environment.

`tf.raw_ops.SparseSegmentSumGrad` triggers a GPU illegal memory access during kernel execution. The first clear error reported is:

`INTERNAL: Failed to launch gpuprim::DeviceRadixSort::SortPairs, temp_storage_bytes: 1status: an illegal memory access was encountered`

After that, the CUDA context appears poisoned and the process eventually aborts with a fatal CHECK failure. The process terminates with `Aborted (core dumped)` / exit code `134`.

This looks like a strong GPU kernel bug rather than a normal input-validation failure.

## Expected behavior

`tf.raw_ops.SparseSegmentSumGrad` should either handle malformed inputs with a regular TensorFlow exception or fail safely, but it should not trigger GPU illegal memory access or poison the process state.

 [CODE_BLOCK] import tensorflow as tf

segment_ids = tf.constant([0, 1], dtype=tf.int32)

### What did you see happen?

When I run `go list -m github.com/pmezard/go-difflib` in workspace mode, I get `v1.0.1-0.20181226105442-5d4384ee4fb2`. According to `go mod graph`, this version seems to come from `go.opentelemetry.io/contrib/detectors/gcp@v1.39.0`, which is a requirement of `google.golang.org/grpc@v1.79.3`. So this version seems to be coming from a transitive test dependency, 3 hops out on the graph.

When I run `GOWORK=off github.com/pmezard/go-difflib` in `a`, I get `v1.0.0`. That matches my expectations.

If I upgrade `a` to `google.golang.org/grpc@v1.79.3` (same as b), then I get `v1.0.0` again. That also matches my expectations, but it's weird that it's different than before. It seems to matter that both root modules have the same required version.

### What did you expect to see?

I expect to get `github.com/pmezard/go-difflib@v1.0.0` in workspace mode because that's the highest required version in the root `go.mod` files and in the `go.mod` files for the immediately required modules. I expect the edge from `google.golang.org/grpc` to `go.opentelemetry.io/contrib/detectors/gcp` to be pruned at either version.

It seems like a larger part of the module graph is expanded in workspace mode when there are requirements on the same module at different versions. I'd kind of expect this to be treated as if that module were only required at the highest version found in the root modules.

I remember this code being incredibly complicated and subtle, so I wouldn't be surprised if this were working-as-intended with a good reason. If that's the case, please consider this a documentation bug: [URL] explains graph pruning in single module mode, and [URL] doesn't say how it should behave differently in workspace mode.

### What did you do?

 On tip (go1.28-devel and also 1.27rc2), the register allocator emits a 3-instruction register swap on every iteration of the scan loop in strings.Fields (and FieldsFunc), where none is needed. The values are already in registers and stay in registers — the swap is pure wasted motion, not due to spilling. 

The following reproducer is taken from the Fields function.

 [CODE_BLOCK] package ssa_test
 
var isDelim = [256]uint8{' ': 1, ',': 1}

//go:noinline
func ScanWords(s string, lens []int) int {
 n := 0
 start := 0
 i := 0
 for i start {
 lens[n] = i - start
 n++
 }
 i++
 start = i
 }
 if i > start {
 lens[n] = i - start
 n++
 }
 return n
}
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 
Running go tool compile -S phicycle_test.go we will see a pattern similar to the following 
``` INCQ DX ; i++
 MOVQ DX, R9 ; \
 MOVQ R8, DX ; } swap DX R8
 MOVQ R9, R8 ; /
 [CODE_BLOCK] — 6 extra MOVQs per non-delimiter byte.
Similar pattern can be seen in ARM64 too 
Edge shuffling seems to cause swapping on the hot path because of regs being flipped while allocating for the two phi vars i, start causing an extra 6 MOV instructions generated every iteration 

Could be related to what is being worked on in [URL]

But since the pattern is a bit different and occurs in Fields function, was not sure if it was the right thing to add it to 80201 hence opening an issue to track 

Other variation of pattern where this is visible

 lens[n] = i - start

 }
 i++
 start = i
 // no continue here — falls through to loop header
 }

 }

}

// Try a version with two explicit continues from different paths
//
//go:noinline
func ScanWords3(s string, lens []int) int {
```

Title: text/template: fatal stack overflow parsing deeply nested {{if}}/{{with}} — control structures left out of the maxStackDepth guard

Body: # text/template: fatal stack overflow parsing deeply nested {{if}}/{{with}} — control structures left out of the maxStackDepth guard

## Summary

`text/template.Parse` (and `html/template.Parse`) crashes the whole process on deeply
nested control structures:

 [CODE_BLOCK] tmpl := strings.Repeat("{{if true}}", 1500000) + "x" + strings.Repeat("{{end}}", 1500000)
template.Parse("", tmpl) // fatal error: stack overflow
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

Verified on go1.23.3 and go1.27.0 (current stable). `{{with}}` behaves identically.
Threshold: 1M nesting parses (11 MB template), 1.5M (16.5 MB) kills the process.

 [CODE_BLOCK] runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit
fatal error: stack overflow
text/template/parse.(*Tree).parseControl (parse.go:531)
 → itemList → textOrAction → action → ifControl → parseControl ...
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

## Root cause / gap in the existing fix

Nested **parentheses** in expressions were capped by CL 671755 (PR #73670, fixing
#71201): `maxStackDepth = 10000`, enforced in `term()` at the `itemLeftParen` case
(master `parse.go:51,820`). Control structures recurse through a different chain —
`parseControl → itemList → textOrAction → action → ifControl/withControl →
parseControl` — which was left out of that fix; no depth counter guards it at HEAD.

## Impact

Any service that parses user-supplied templates (theme engines, mail-merge, report
generators, AI-agent frameworks executing model-emitted templates) is process-killed
by one template. The crash is a fatal runtime error — unrecoverable by the caller.

I'm aware the docs position template authors as trusted (added alongside the parens
fix), but #71201 — the identical class on the parens path — was accepted and fixed
with a Security label, and this is the same bug one AST level up.

## Suggested fix

Track control-structure nesting in `parseControl` with the same `maxStackDepth`
budget (increment on entry, decrement on exit), returning the existing
"exceeded max nesting depth" style error. Happy to send the CL/PR — PoCs for both
text and html variants are ready.

**Go version:** verified on go1.23.3 and go1.27.0 (current stable); master parse.go checked.

Title: archive, image, debug, encoding, x/net/html: DO NOT PANIC

Body: We have a number of packages that implement parsers where a panic might lead to a Denial of Service, but returning an invalid input error instead would be perfectly harmless. We should wrap them all in a `recover()` and prevent the panic from propagating, as a robustness and defense in depth measure.

We need to be careful about preserving documented panic conditions, and about not leaving behind persistent state that might be corrupt following a panic.

Ideas for other packages that can benefit are welcome. Crypto packages were intentionally left out, as we should be confident in their operation. `math/big` has a lot of entry points and persistent state by definition (and we have a plan to drag it out of the security perimeter).

/cc @golang/security

### What did you do?

`Decoder.Token` was fixed in #74750 to keep reporting a bare `io.EOF` when the input is a truncated prefix of a valid JSON value, matching v1. That fix is bypassed if `Decoder.More` is called first.

 [CODE_BLOCK] package main

import (
 "encoding/json"
 "fmt"
 "strings"
)

func main() {
 for _, callMore := range []bool{false, true} {
 dec := json.NewDecoder(strings.NewReader(`[1,`))
 dec.Token() // [
 dec.Token() // 1
 if callMore {
 dec.More()
 }
 _, err := dec.Token()
 fmt.Printf("More=%-5v err=%#v InputOffset=%d\n", callMore, err, dec.InputOffset())
 }
}
 [/CODE_BLOCK]

 [CODE_BLOCK] More=false err=&errors.errorString{s:"EOF"} InputOffset=3
More=true err=&json.SyntaxError{msg:"unexpected end of JSON input", Offset:3} InputOffset=2
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

The same divergence occurs at every truncation point that leaves a valid prefix; `{`, `{"a"`, `{"a":` and `{"a":1,` all behave like `[1,` above.

The two rows to agree, as they do with `GOEXPERIMENT=nojsonv2`:

 [CODE_BLOCK] More=false err=&errors.errorString{s:"EOF"} InputOffset=3
More=true err=&errors.errorString{s:"EOF"} InputOffset=3
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

`Decoder.More` is documented only to report whether there is another element in the current array or object. It is not documented to affect the error subsequently reported by `Decoder.Token`, and under the v1 implementation it does not.

Title: doc/godebug.md: urlstrictcolons description is out of date for Go 1.27

Body: ### Go version

go1.27.0

### What did you do

The `urlstrictcolons` entry in `doc/godebug.md` is unchanged from Go 1.26:
> Go 1.26 added a new `urlstrictcolons` setting that controls whether `net/url.Parse`
> allows malformed hostnames containing colons outside of a bracketed IPv6 address.
> The default `urlstrictcolons=1` rejects URLs such as `[URL] or `[URL]

CL 758900 ("net/url: permit colons in the host subcomponent of non-http/https URLs", for #78077) limited that validation to http and https, so as of Go 1.27 the setting has no effect on other schemes.

 [CODE_BLOCK] package main

import (
 "fmt"
 "net/url"
)

func main() {
 for _, s := range []string{"[URL] "ftp://localhost:1:2", "mongodb://h:1,h2:2"} {
 _, err := url.Parse(s)
 fmt.Printf("%-24q accepted=%v\n", s, err == nil)
 }
}
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

Run with `GODEBUG=urlstrictcolons=1` on go1.27.0:

 [CODE_BLOCK] "[URL] accepted=false
"ftp://localhost:1:2" accepted=true
"mongodb://h:1,h2:2" accepted=true
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### What did you see happen

The setting applies only to http and https. The two non-http URLs are accepted whether `urlstrictcolons` is 1, 0, or unset.

### What did you expect to see

The documentation describes the setting as controlling whether `net/url.Parse` allows colons in hostnames, without qualification, so it reads as though it governs colon-bearing hosts generally. Since the scheme restriction is the substance of the Go 1.27 change, it seems worth stating in the entry, and the Go 1.27 release notes do not mention it either.

Happy to send a CL if a wording change is wanted.

Title: net/http: Transport should allow disabling Accept-Encoding: gzip on a per-request basis

Body: The net/http `Transport` automatically adds an "Accept-Encoding: gzip" header and transparently decompresses any compressed response, except when `Transport.DisableCompression` is set or the user sets `Accept-Encoding` manually.

Setting an empty Accept-Encoding value in the headers map should prevent the `Transport` from adding one, in the same way setting an empty Content-Length value prevents one from being automatically added in various places.

 [CODE_BLOCK] req.Header["Accept-Encoding"] = nil // prevent Transport from adding "gzip"
 [/CODE_BLOCK]

Body: ### Go version

### What did you do?

**_This was first observed in the Go CI/CD builder on ppc64le POWER10, and I then reproduced it locally on a POWER10 system using current Go master._** Link

On a ppc64le POWER10 system, I checked out current Go master and ran the full test suite with `GOPPC64=power10`.

The failure reproduces locally in:

 [CODE_BLOCK] TestScript/cgo_path_space_quote
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

I then reproduced the test directly with:

 [CODE_BLOCK] GOPPC64=power10 ./bin/go test cmd/go \
 -run='TestScript/cgo_path_space_quote' \
 -count=1 -v
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

The test sets `CC` to a wrapper executable whose path contains spaces, followed by `clang`, for example:

 [CODE_BLOCK] "/tmp/.../program files/which cc" clang
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

I also verified independently that the compiler supports the Power10 flag:

 [CODE_BLOCK] clang -m64 -mcpu=power10 /tmp/p10.c -o /tmp/p10
echo $?
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

which returns:

 [CODE_BLOCK] 0
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### What did you see happen?

`TestScript/cgo_path_space_quote` fails during `go run .` with:

 [CODE_BLOCK] # test
.../pkg/tool/linux_ppc64le/link: The external toolchain does not support -mcpu=power10. This is required to externally link GOPPC64 >= power10
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

The test itself successfully preserves the multi-word `CC` value:

 [CODE_BLOCK] "/tmp/.../program files/which cc" clang
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

To inspect the Power10 capability probe, I temporarily instrumented `linkerFlagSupported`. The failing probe executed:

 [CODE_BLOCK] DEBUG linkerFlagSupported: flag="-mcpu=power10"
cmd=["/tmp/.../program files/which cc"
 "-m64"
 "-o" "..."
 "-mcpu=power10"
 ".../trivial.c"]
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

The trailing `clang` argument from `CC` is missing.

The corresponding call site passes only `argv[0]`:

 [CODE_BLOCK] linkerFlagSupported(ctxt.Arch, argv[0], "", "-mcpu=power10")
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

while `linkerFlagSupported` later executes:

 [CODE_BLOCK] exec.Command(linker, flags...)
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

As a result, the wrapper is invoked without the trailing compiler argument, causing the flag probe to return false.

The compiler itself does support the flag:

 [CODE_BLOCK] $ clang -m64 -mcpu=power10 /tmp/p10.c -o /tmp/p10
$ echo $?
0
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### What did you expect to see?

`TestScript/cgo_path_space_quote` should pass when `CC` contains a quoted executable path followed by additional arguments.

In this case, the external linker command is effectively:

 [CODE_BLOCK] "/tmp/.../program files/which cc" clang
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

Flag probing should preserve the complete external linker command, including the trailing `clang` argument.

The Power10 capability probe should therefore invoke the wrapper with `clang` before `-mcpu=power10`, detect that the compiler supports the flag, and allow `go run .` to complete successfully.

Title: x/pkgsite: request to exclude 55 abandoned pre-release dd-trace-go/v2/contrib/* pseudo-versions from the Directories listing

Body: Following up on #74016, which stalled on an open question. I think we finally have a definitive answer, so a fresh, narrower issue seemed cleaner than reviving that whole thread.

### Background

We restructured our `v2` line so each `contrib` integration is its own module, published at `github.com/DataDog/dd-trace-go/contrib/ /v2` (major-version suffix at the end of the path). Before we landed on that layout, an earlier pre-release arrangement briefly put the same integrations at `github.com/DataDog/dd-trace-go/v2/contrib/ ` instead, with the major version in the middle of the path and no trailing suffix, so those modules never got a version at all. We dropped that layout before our first stable tag and never meant to publish it.

pkg.go.dev had already crawled these modules once, though. Each one is still sitting in the index as a single pseudo-version: the proxy returns an empty `@v/list` and a 404 on `@latest`, but still resolves the exact version directly if you ask for it:

 [CODE_BLOCK] $ curl -s [URL]
{"Version":"v0.0.0-20240517154620-1bc2693d3082", ...}
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

The result: [URL] currently lists 55 entries under "Directories," all pointing at these dead, year-and-a-half-old paths. None of it matches how the module is actually laid out today.

### Retraction doesn't help here

I went digging to see if we could fix this ourselves with `retract` directives. We can't, at least not through this code path.

`GetNestedModules` (`internal/postgres/details.go`) reads straight from the `modules` table with no retraction filter at all. That only kicks in later, in the latest-version resolution path (`IsRetracted`, `internal/postgres/version.go`). Retracting would also mean recreating 55 dead `go.mod` files at the old layout just to publish retracting versions for modules nobody should be pulling in anyway. That's a lot of churn for nothing.

### What would actually work

`GetNestedModules` does call `db.IsExcluded(ctx, mi.ModulePath, mi.Version)` on every row before it makes the listing, and `excludes()` (`internal/postgres/excluded.go`) already supports exact `module@version` patterns.

Each of these 55 modules only ever had one pseudo-version published. An exact `module@version` exclusion per module would clear all of them out without touching anything else. Importantly, it wouldn't also match the live `github.com/DataDog/dd-trace-go/v2/contrib` package path, which a plain prefix exclusion would risk doing.

Above is extracted from vmlinux (compiled by clang-15) by llvm-dwarfdump-15, when linux kernel compiled with DWARF5 debug info, go debug/dwarf can't decode entry at 0x000160e6 correctly.

Test program
```
package main

import (
 "fmt"
 "debug/dwarf"
 "debug/elf"
)

func main() {
 file, err := elf.Open("vmlinux")
 if err != nil {
 return
 }
 debugInfo, err := file.DWARF()
 if err != nil {
 return
 }

 ent, _ := getEntryByOffset(debugInfo, 0x000142a2)
 fmt.Printf("%v\n", ent)
 ent, _ = getEntryByOffset(debugInfo, 0x000160e6)
 fmt.Printf("%v\n", ent)
}

func getEntryByOffset(debugInfo *dwarf.Data, offset dwarf.Offset) (*dwarf.Entry, error) {
 r := debugInfo.Reader()
 r.Seek(offset)
 return r.Next()
}
```

### What did you expect to see?
The 2nd printf should print ent name as rcu_read_unlock.

### What did you see instead?
The 2nd printf should print ent name of some other subprogram.
